propositions.text: This appeal arises from the Federal Court decision dismissing the appellant's judicial review application for lack of jurisdiction under section 18.1 of the Federal Courts Act.
propositions.quote: This appeal arises from a decision of the Federal Court ... dismissing the appellant’s application for judicial review as it did not challenge a matter within the scope of section 18.1 of the Federal Courts Act

propositions.text: The Federal Court also dismissed the appellant's mandamus application for failure to identify a public legal duty on the RCMP Commissioner.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court also dismissed the appellant’s application for mandamus as the appellant failed to identify a public legal duty to act on the part of the respondent Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) Commissioner.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the appeal arises from the Federal Court dismissing the appellant's judicial review and mandamus applications for lack of jurisdiction and public legal duty.

propositions.text: The Federal Court found the appellant's affidavits disjointed and difficult to piece together chronologically.
propositions.quote: the appellant’s “disjointed affidavits that mixed random and selective facts, hearsay, allegations and submission”

propositions.text: The appellant's sister and brother-in-law were involved in lengthy family law proceedings in Alberta, with abuse allegations made to the RCMP.
propositions.quote: the appellant’s sister and then brother-in-law became embroiled in lengthy divorce, custody, and access proceedings ... The appellant’s sister subsequently made allegations of domestic and child abuse against her then husband to the RCMP.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Federal Court found the appellant's affidavits disjointed and that the appellant's sister was involved in family law proceedings with abuse allegations to the RCMP.

propositions.text: In February 2021, the appellant filed complaints to the CRCC requesting investigation of the RCMP's conduct regarding her sister's allegations.
propositions.quote: In February 2021, the appellant filed two complaints to the Civilian Review and Complaints Commission for the RCMP (CRCC) requesting that it investigate the RCMP’s conduct in its response to her sister’s allegations.

propositions.text: The RCMP Act allows complaints about RCMP members' conduct in performing duties.
propositions.quote: Under the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act ... an individual may make a complaint concerning the conduct of a member of the RCMP in the performance of a duty or function (RCMP Act, s. 45.53(1)).

propositions.text: The mandate and procedures of the CRCC are described in British Columbia Civil Liberties Association v. Canada (Royal Mounted Police).
propositions.quote: A review of the mandate and procedures of the CRCC can be found in British Columbia Civil Liberties Association v. Canada (Royal Mounted Police), 2021 FC 1475 at paras. 7-8

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appellant filed complaints to the CRCC in 2021 about RCMP conduct, under the RCMP Act's complaint provisions, with CRCC's mandate described in prior case law.

propositions.text: The appellant requested the CRCC address management issues in two RCMP detachments, which was beyond CRCC's jurisdiction and referred to the Commissioner.
propositions.quote: The appellant also requested the CRCC address “the overall management and conduct of the Cochrane and Airdrie detachments ...” The CRCC did not address this issue as it was beyond its jurisdiction and referred the appellant’s request ... to the Commissioner.

propositions.text: The management allegation was directed to the RCMP's OISP for internal administrative review.
propositions.quote: This allegation was then directed to the RCMP’s Office of Investigative Standards and Practices (OISP) for an internal administrative review.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the appellant's management complaint was outside CRCC jurisdiction and referred to the Commissioner and OISP for internal review.

propositions.text: In April to June 2023, the appellant sent emails to the Commissioner requesting disclosure of the OISP review and clarification on its disclosure in family law proceedings.
propositions.quote: In April, May and June 2023, the appellant sent the Commissioner several emails, requesting disclosure of the OISP review ... requested confirmation that the OISP review would be disclosed in family law proceedings

propositions.text: On June 19, the appellant requested responses to 20 questions about the OISP review of detachment mismanagement.
propositions.quote: In a June 19th email the appellant requested “response and clarification” to 20 questions the appellant had concerning the OISP review of the allegation of mismanagement of the detachments.

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts the appellant's 2023 emails to the Commissioner seeking disclosure and answers about the OISP review and detachment management.

propositions.text: The June 19 email set a June 23 deadline for response, warning non-response would be considered a reviewable decision.
propositions.quote: The June 19th email set a deadline for response of June 23, 2023, failing which the appellant would consider the RCMP's lack of response to be a reviewable decision.

propositions.text: The appellant alleged that as of June 19, 2023, the RCMP Commissioner made a reviewable decision not to address ongoing conduct related to her complaint.
propositions.quote: as of June 19, 2023, the RCMP Commissioner and/or the RCMP have made the reviewable decision to not address the ongoing conduct of the RCMP relating to my [Public Complaint] and matters relating to same.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the appellant's June 19 email set a response deadline and alleged the RCMP made a reviewable decision not to address ongoing conduct.

propositions.text: The Department of Justice responded seeking clarification of the appellant's request and whether she was counsel in the family law proceeding.
propositions.quote: The Department of Justice responded to the June 19th email on behalf of the Commissioner. Counsel sought clarification of the appellant’s request as well as confirmation whether she had been retained as counsel in the Alberta Court of King’s Bench proceeding.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Department of Justice responded seeking clarification and appellant's status in family law proceedings.

propositions.text: Shortly after, the appellant filed the judicial review application dismissed by Lafrenière J.
propositions.quote: Shortly thereafter, the appellant filed the judicial review application that came before Lafrenière J.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the appellant filed the judicial review application shortly after the Department of Justice response.

propositions.text: The Federal Court judge noted the relief sought was narrowed to a declaration of breach, setting aside the decision, and mandamus to investigate misconduct and mismanagement.
propositions.quote: the broad relief sought in the notice of application had been whittled down ... to a declaration that the Commissioner breached his duty ... an order setting aside the alleged decision, and an order for mandamus directing the Commissioner to address and investigate the alleged issues of misconduct and mismanagement

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court judge noted the narrowed relief sought included breach declaration, setting aside decision, and mandamus to investigate misconduct.

propositions.text: Jurisdiction under subsection 18.1(1) of the Federal Courts Act is assessed on a correctness standard.
propositions.quote: Questions as to what constitutes a “matter” within subsection 18.1(1) of the Federal Courts Act go to the jurisdiction of the Court and are assessed on the standard of correctness

propositions.text: Mandamus's first criterion, existence of a public legal duty, is reviewed on correctness; other criteria on palpable and overriding error.
propositions.quote: the first criterion for mandamus, namely whether there is a public legal duty, is assessed on a correctness basis, with the balance of the mandamus criteria raising questions of mixed fact and law reviewable on a standard of palpable and overriding error

paragraphs.summary: The court explains jurisdiction under section 18.1 and mandamus criteria are reviewed on correctness and palpable error standards.

propositions.text: The court finds no error in the Federal Court's reasons.
propositions.quote: I see no error in the reasons of the Federal Court.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no error in the Federal Court's reasons.

propositions.text: A matter not affecting legal rights, obligations, or prejudicial effects is not reviewable.
propositions.quote: a matter that fails to affect legal rights, impose legal obligations, or cause prejudicial effects is not reviewable

propositions.text: The Commissioner's lack of response to the June 19 email was not a reviewable decision as it did not affect legal rights, impose obligations, or cause prejudicial effects.
propositions.quote: The Commissioner’s lack of response to the appellant’s June 19th email did not constitute a reviewable decision as it did not affect the appellant’s legal rights, impose legal obligations, or have prejudicial effects.

propositions.text: The appellant had no legal right to answers, the Commissioner had no legal duty to respond, and non-response had no prejudicial effects.
propositions.quote: The appellant had no legal right to be provided with answers to her questions, the Commissioner had no legal duty or obligation to respond to the appellant’s questions, and the non-response did not have prejudicial effects.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Commissioner's non-response was not reviewable as it did not affect legal rights or duties, nor cause prejudice.

propositions.text: The Commissioner had no legal duty to conduct the OISP internal review, nor did its results affect the appellant's legal rights.
propositions.quote: The Commissioner was under no legal duty to conduct an internal review of the allegations, nor do the results of that review, if any, affect the appellant’s legal rights.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no legal duty or rights affected by the OISP internal review or its results.

propositions.text: The appellant argues judicial review is essential to hold the RCMP accountable for allegedly misleading the Alberta Court of King’s Bench.
propositions.quote: The appellant places considerable emphasis on the importance of judicial review to ensure that public officers conduct themselves according to law and argues that judicial review is the only way in which the RCMP can be held accountable for what she says was misleading the Alberta Court of King’s Bench.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues judicial review is necessary to hold the RCMP accountable for alleged misleading conduct.

propositions.text: The court rejects the appellant's argument, noting a similar argument was rejected in Democracy Watch 2009 regarding the Ethics Commissioner’s duty to investigate.
propositions.quote: The argument was rejected by this Court which concluded that the Ethics Commissioner had no duty to investigate beyond that prescribed by statute.

propositions.text: The Ethics Commissioner had no statutory duty to investigate beyond the statute, and refusal to investigate did not affect applicant's rights.
propositions.quote: The refusal to investigate did not affect the applicant’s rights and the Ethics Commission was under no statutory duty to act on the applicant’s request.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects the appellant's argument, citing Democracy Watch 2009 where no duty to investigate beyond statute was found.

propositions.text: Parliament creates formal complaints procedures with express duties on public officers to investigate.
propositions.quote: Where Parliament creates a formal complaints procedure with a concomitant duty on an agent of Parliament or public officer to investigate, it does so expressly

propositions.text: The CRCC process does not create a general complaints procedure imposing legal obligations beyond statute, such as demands in the June 19 email.
propositions.quote: In establishing the CRCC process, Parliament did not create a general complaints procedure that gave rise to a legal obligation on the Commissioner to respond to demands beyond the scope of what is required by statute

propositions.text: By statute, the appellant had the right to file a complaint, have it investigated, and receive a response, which she has now received.
propositions.quote: By statute, the appellant had a right to file a complaint, to have it investigated and to receive a response, which she now has.

propositions.text: The question of the appellant's standing to file a complaint was not raised before the court.
propositions.quote: the question whether the appellant, who was neither the spouse nor the mother at the center of the domestic and child abuse allegations, had standing to file a complaint was not raised before us.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the CRCC process imposes no legal duty beyond statute; the appellant had statutory complaint rights and standing was not challenged.

propositions.text: The RCMP delivered a detailed report on the appellant's 14 allegations on January 25, 2024, concluding the investigation was complete and advising of CRCC review rights.
propositions.quote: The RCMP delivered its report on the two complaints on January 25, 2024. It addressed each of the appellant’s 14 allegations in considerable detail. The report concluded: ... the investigation into this complaint has now been concluded ... you may request a review by the CRCC ... within 60 days

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the RCMP delivered a detailed report concluding the investigation and advising the appellant of CRCC review rights.

propositions.text: The court next considers the appellant's request for an order of mandamus.
propositions.quote: I turn next to the request for an order of mandamus.

paragraphs.summary: The court proceeds to consider the appellant's mandamus request.

propositions.text: The Federal Court concluded the appellant did not meet the mandamus test requiring a public legal duty and clear right to performance.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court concluded that the appellant did not meet the test for mandamus set out in Apotex. That test requires the appellant establish, inter alia, that the Commissioner owed her a public legal duty to act, and that she has a clear right to the Commissioner’s performance of that duty.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court found the appellant failed to meet the mandamus test requiring a public legal duty and clear right.

propositions.text: The appellant cites RCMP Act s.5(1) as source of legal right to have the Commissioner respond and investigate misconduct allegations.
propositions.quote: The appellant cites subsection 5(1) of the RCMP Act, which grants the Commissioner the responsibility and authority for the management and control of the RCMP, as the source of the legal right to have the Commissioner respond to her questions and investigate the allegations of systemic misconduct in the Cochrane and Airdrie detachments.

propositions.text: The appellant contends a public legal duty arises from common law police duties described in R. v. Godoy.
propositions.quote: The appellant also contends that a public legal duty to act arises from the common law duties of police as described by the Supreme Court in R. v. Godoy, such as preservation of the peace, the prevention of crime and the protection of life and property

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the RCMP Act and common law police duties create a public legal duty to respond and investigate misconduct allegations.

propositions.text: These arguments fail.
propositions.quote: These arguments fail.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that these arguments fail.

propositions.text: Subsection 5(1) grants the Commissioner authority for RCMP management and control.
propositions.quote: Subsection 5(1) is the source of the Commissioner’s authority for the management and control of the RCMP.

propositions.text: Statutory authority to a public official does not create a legal right for citizens to demand exercise of discretion in a certain way absent effect on a legal right.
propositions.quote: Absent an effect on a legally cognizable right or interest, a grant of statutory authority to a public official does not give rise to a legal right on the part of a citizen to require that the associated administrative discretion of management and control be exercised in a certain way, or at all (see, for example, Reisdorf v. Canada, 2023 FCA 188 at para. 8).

propositions.text: No error in Federal Court's finding that Commissioner had no legal obligation to respond within the unilateral, arbitrary, and extremely short deadline in June 19th email.
propositions.quote: There is therefore no error in the Federal Court’s finding that “the Commissioner had no legal obligation to respond within the unilateral, arbitrary and extremely short deadline” imposed in the June 19th email (Federal Court Decision, at para. 27).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains subsection 5(1) authority and agrees with the Federal Court that the Commissioner had no legal obligation to meet the short deadline.

propositions.text: The appellant's reliance on common law police duties does not help her position.
propositions.quote: The appellant’s reliance on the common law duties of the police does not assist her position.

propositions.text: Common law duties do not impose a positive duty on the Commissioner to respond to the appellant's email.
propositions.quote: Whatever the scope of those duties, they do not translate into a positive duty on the part of the Commissioner to respond to the appellant's email.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that common law police duties do not impose a duty on the Commissioner to respond to the appellant's email.

propositions.text: The appeal is dismissed with costs fixed at $2,500.
propositions.quote: The appeal will therefore be dismissed with costs which I would fix in the all-inclusive amount of $2,500.

propositions.text: Judges Rennie, Gleason, and Locke agree with the dismissal and costs order.
propositions.quote: “Donald J. Rennie” J.A. “I agree. Mary J.L. Gleason J.A.” “I agree. George R. Locke J.A.”

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal with costs of $2,500 and all judges concur.
